newsitem.title: CROATIA: Opposition cries foul before Croatia vote.
newsitem.headline: Opposition cries foul before Croatia vote.

text.p: Two candidates challenging President Franjo Tudjman, who is expected to win re-election easily on Sunday, alleged on Thursday that irregularities had already put the fairness of the outcome in doubt.
Croatians are set to elect a president for the second time since the former Yugoslav republic gained independence in 1991 under the leadership of Franjo Tudjman.

The campaign, which officially ends on Friday night, has been marked by constant complaints of irregularities by his rivals -- Vlado Gotovac of the Social Liberal party (HSLS) and Social Democrat leader Zdravko Tomac.

"Our first complaint is complete unfairness in the candidates' access to state-controlled media and the other is absolute partiality of the state electoral commission, which rejected all our demands and complaints," Stjepo Martinovic, spokesman for Gotovac's election team, told Reuters.
Analysts believe Tudjman will be easily re-elected in the first round of voting, with little chance for Gotovac and Tomac to upset his 'Father of the Nation' appeal.
The HSLS said it would not be granted permission to monitor several polling stations, which it said had in the past proved crucial in tipping the final balance.
"This is voting aboard ships, in prisons and abroad," Martinovic said. Some 300,000 Croats in neighbouring Bosnia and thousands more overseas are eligible to vote on Sunday.

"We can already say the voting will be irregular and it will certainly not be a festival of democracy, although there is no war, no state of emergency except that in the minds of the HDZ leaders," he said.
The HSLS further complained Tudjman was using his official position for campaigning on state television, from which most Croatians get their daily news. The complaint was rejected.

"During the electoral campaign, (Tudjman's) birthday party was celebrated as state holiday. A military parade hailed Tudjman as its supreme commander. On statehood day (May 30) he was praised as the man who had created Croatia," said an HSLS statement faxed to Reuters.

The commission also rejected Gotovac's demand that campaigning be prolonged for two weeks so he could make up for the days he spent resting after injury. There were no legal grounds to accept the demand, the commission said.

A Croatian army officer hit Gotovac on the head with a belt buckle during a rally last week and the HSLS leader was ordered by doctors to stay in bed. He briefly appeared at an HSLS rally in Zagreb and will attend two more before Sunday.

In another controversy, Social Democrat leader Tomac was not allowed to hold a rally on Zagreb's main square on Friday. City authorities decided campaigning in the capital should end on Thursday night, when Tudjman holds his rally.
"I am therefore not an equal candidate," Tomac told a news conference. "It's apparently thought in this country that everything begins and ends with Tudjman," he said.
Rallies in Zagreb are crucial as the city has over one million inhabitants -- almost one quarter of the whole of Croatia. But Tomac said the refusal would not upset him.
"I am convinced that Zagrebians will know how to respond to this act, (which) only proves that the time has come to move on...I am a healthy candidate who can heal the sick Croatia."
The 75-year old Tudjman, said to be suffering from cancer, said in a pre-election television interview on Wednesday he was confident his victory was in sight.

"(My victory) is not in question," he said. "I am definitely going to win -- this is not my own estimate but (Croatian) people are showing me this all the time. My two opponents together...will get half of the votes that I'll get."
